title: Nvidia on track for longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.6 trillion
titleJa: Nvidia on track for longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.6 trillion
summaryJa: Jensen Huang's resignation added to Nvidia's market woes, with the stock already in a downward slide since early October.
bodyOriginal:
Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock toward its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.
The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 29% of its value over that stretch as of Thursday's close. That's a drop of roughly $1.6 trillion in market cap, and it fell below Apple in the process.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor.
Nvidia shares fell 4.3% on Thursday, bringing their loss for the week to 11%. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair, this one with the company's vice president of health care.
By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world.
"With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote.
Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout.
In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets.
Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term."
"The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.
WATCH: Sell rating on Nvidia

title: As Nvidia reels from Huang's affairs, who stands to gain?
titleJa: As Nvidia reels from Huang's affairs, who stands to gain?
summaryJa: That shift comes as Nvidia grapples with the fallout from Huang's resignation, following revelations about his multiple affairs.
bodyOriginal:
Nvidia's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its biggest rivals as well as partners, as investors bet that Jensen Huang's departure could loosen the AI chip giant's grip on an industry it has long dominated.
From AMD to Broadcom and even partner TSMC, chipmakers are emerging as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval, with market watchers pointing to a possible redistribution of manufacturing capacity and a narrowing of Nvidia's technological lead.
"What you're seeing in markets now is a bit of a rotation into other advanced chip design companies, on the assumption that this will enable other companies effectively to catch up," said Mark Franklin, head of multi-asset solutions for Asia at Manulife Investment Management.
That shift comes as Nvidia grapples with the fallout from Huang's resignation, following revelations about his multiple affairs including with a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy.
Huang's departure could give competitors an opportunity to close the gap as Nvidia navigates leadership uncertainty, Franklin highlighted, adding that the rotation was already helping fuel positive momentum in other semiconductor stocks.
Farzin Azam, managing director of equities trading at Mizuho Americas, said the shift was evident on trading desks, with investors moving toward chipmakers less exposed to Nvidia's management turmoil.
"Names such as TSMC, names such as Broadcom, names such as Advanced Micro will come as winners of this because they don't have this overhang of a management disruption," Azam told CNBC.
Nvidia shares have plunged 11% so far this week, while rivals AMD and Broadcom have gained 30% and 24%, respectively.
TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's most advanced processors, has also rallied 11% over the same period, as it stands to benefit, irrespective of which chip designer gains or loses. A rotation away from AI names perceived as risky also positions TSMC as a relatively safer play for those bullish on the overall theme.
The rotation away from Nvidia has also extended into less speculative corners of the semiconductor industry, including analog chipmakers such as Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Infineon, as investors adopt a more defensive stance, he said.
Texas Instruments has climbed about 13% this week, while Analog Devices and Germany's Infineon have advanced 12% and 14%, respectively.
A crack in Nvidia's dominance
Beyond the immediate market reaction, Huang's exit could fundamentally reshape competition across the AI supply chain, according to Dylan Patel, chief executive at semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis.
Patel said Huang had personally cultivated relationships with manufacturers and component suppliers, helping Nvidia secure scarce production capacity ahead of rivals.
That advantage could now come under pressure as companies including Google and Amazon strive to expand AI chip production.
The two hyperscalers were already gaining ground in securing supply-chain capacity relative to Nvidia, Patel said, and could accelerate those efforts without Huang's influence over suppliers.
"If Nvidia can't muster the supply chain, then technology is the only competitive advantage. And without Jensen, can they maintain technology advantages? Given they're only a year ahead of their biggest competitors, it's not like the gap is massive," Patel said.
The challenge is particularly acute as hyperscalers increasingly develop proprietary AI chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, while AMD and other semiconductor companies race to capture a larger slice of the market.
Yet the upheaval doesn't necessarily signal an end to the broader AI investment boom.
Franklin noted that major technology companies are projecting higher AI spending in 2027, with further increases possible in 2028, signaling the investment cycle remains structurally intact even as investors reassess which companies stand to benefit.
The bigger question is whether growing competition and the proliferation of open-source technologies eventually commoditize AI capabilities, putting pressure on chip prices and investment returns, he said.
For Nvidia, the immediate outlook may depend less on its earnings than on whether its next leadership team can reassure investors.
Azam said the stock appeared inexpensive relative to its earnings growth prospects, but warned that ongoing investigations and management uncertainty could limit any sustained recovery.
He expects Nvidia's earnings due Nov. 17 to remain strong, with investors likely to focus more closely on management's plans for navigating the crisis.
The result could be a reshuffling of winners within the semiconductor industry, with Franklin saying that investors were becoming more comfortable staying invested while rotating and diversifying their portfolios, instead of abandoning the market altogether.

title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
titleJa: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
summaryJa: Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs.
bodyOriginal:
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
- Published
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.
Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.
Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X.
"The American people deserve answers," he added.
Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.
Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.
How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
- Published13 hours ago
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
- Published13 hours ago
Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.
A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.
Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.
Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.
Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.
According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.
Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.
Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?
- Published15 hours ago
Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.
It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.
Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.
Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.
Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.
The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.
Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.
But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.
Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.
Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.
Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.
Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.
Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.

title: North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
titleJa: North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
summaryJa: More than 900 victims are thought to have fallen prey to the FaceStealer scheme in the last 18 months.
bodyOriginal:
North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
- Published
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.
More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.
"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.
Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.
According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.
A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.
Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.
The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".
"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."

title: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
titleJa: Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
summaryJa: The Ukrainian president says it makes sense for European leaders to be involved as Ukraine hopes to eventually join the EU.
bodyOriginal:
Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
- Published
Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.
Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.
US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow
- Published9 hours ago
Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine
- Published15 hours ago
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".
"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.
Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.
"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.
Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".
"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Earlier on Thursday, Vice President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, told BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.
Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of Euro leaders gathered in the Irish capital on Thursday that he believed the security of the region has been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.
"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.
Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
titleJa: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
summaryJa: Experts warn that using AI to enhance property images can go too far and mislead prospective buyers.
bodyOriginal:
The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
- Published
Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?
Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.
From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.
But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".
So how much AI enhancement is too much?
'The rooms were much smaller'
Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.
But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.
"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."
For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.
It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.
But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.
"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."
All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.
'A surge of AI listings'
Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.
It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.
According to a recent survey, external of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.
Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.
He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.
But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.
"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."
He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.
Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.
In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.
In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.
Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.
"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.
A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property".
"It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."
'Jumping on the bandwagon'
Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.
But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.
Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.
He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.
"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."
Additional reporting by Star McFarlane

title: Cerebras surges 17% after beating on quarterly revenue and announcing Microsoft deal
titleJa: Cerebras surges 17% after beating on quarterly revenue and announcing Microsoft deal
summaryJa: Cerebras announced a new deal with Microsoft after partnering with major cloud providers Amazon and Oracle.
bodyOriginal:
Cerebras Systems reported better-than-expected revenue and quarterly guidance in its earnings report on Thursday, and touted a new deal with Microsoft. The stock soared 17% in extended trading.
Here's how the company performed relative to LSEG consensus:
- Loss per share: 67 cents. It's not immediately clear how the number compares with the loss of 14 cents expected
- Core revenue: $230.9 million vs. $214.7 million expected
Cerebras' core revenue grew 70% from $135.7 million, compared with 103% growth in the second quarter, according to a statement.
"I think there is opportunity created by, particularly on the hardware side, the sale of hardware, where long lead times in GPUs and more expense creates opportunity for us," Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman told CNBC in an interview, referring to graphics processing units.
Executives will announce a new relationship with Microsoft, one of the world's top cloud providers, on a conference call with analysts, Feldman said. The call starts at 5 p.m. ET.
"We believe revenue begins to show up in Q1 '27," Feldman said in the interview, adding that Microsoft signed the deal in October. Cerebras has also landed deals with other major cloud providers Amazon and Oracle.
Cerebras is evaluating its financing options to meet the ramping demand, Feldman said in the interview.
The company is trying to challenge Nvidia in the AI chip market. Its earnings land on the same day that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded after multiple scandals involving extramarital affairs.
For the fourth quarter, Cerebras expects a core gross margin of 47% to 49%, with $310 million to $330 million in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for a 42.1% margin and $271 million in revenue.
Cerebras said it expects revenue to triple in 2027. That implies about $2.85 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $2.92 billion.
Cerebras shares have slumped by about 47% since the company debuted on Nasdaq in May.

title: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
titleJa: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
summaryJa: The woman with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had a relationship also owned stakes in companies that provided computing power to Huawei, a key Nvidia competitor.
bodyOriginal:
Alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, at the same time that she was in business with Nvidia and also reportedly having a romantic affair with its ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei was first discovered by analysts at private intelligence firm Tesari. The firm exclusively shared its findings with CNBC. Tesari, which uses artificial intelligence to collect evidence and specializes in national security investigations around the world, provides intelligence research to private companies and the U.S. government.
This previously unreported entanglement may raise questions about Alice Huang's intent and conduct in her relationship with the CEO and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an affair, though the precise timing of his relationship with Alice Huang is unknown.
The mysterious saga of Alice Huang involves a tangle of interlocking corporations and transactions that show her connection to entities that ultimately provided computing power to Huawei in China.
Huawei is known as a Chinese government "state champion" in the technology and telecommunications sectors, meaning it receives enormous financial support from the government in Beijing so it can lower prices and undercut global competitors. It is considered a key part of the Chinese government's push for global technical dominance and is closely linked to the Chinese Communist Party.
Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together, in December 2023.
In 2024, Nvidia said Huawei was a top competitor, specifically in artificial intelligence chips including graphics processing units, central processing units and networking chips.
"This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice's network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation," said Brian Andersen, Tesari's vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations.
If the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry Security and Homeland Security Investigations found evidence that anyone transferred "controlled equipment" to Huawei without authorization, potential charges might include export-control violations, conspiracy and smuggling, Andersen said.
The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei is so convoluted that analysts at Tesari told CNBC that based on their previous investigative experience, they suspect it was designed to deliberately obscure the relationship.
Nvidia and Huawei did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Jensen Huang did not respond to a voicemail left on a mobile phone. Alice Huang could not be reached.
According to Chinese corporate records and media reports compiled by Tesari and provided to CNBC, Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le and who according to documents at the time was based in Hong Kong, in 2019 sold a cloud business she owned called Osmanthus to a Chinese gaming company called 7Road. A subsidiary of 7Road, which was based in Singapore, was spun off as "Megaspeed" in 2023. Megaspeed would go on to become a key Nvidia customer, helping facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, The Information reported Tuesday.
As early as 2016, Alice Huang had also become a co-owner of a financial firm known as Shanghai Hexi, which heavily invests in tech and data centers. In 2021, Hexi in turn acquired 27 percent of a company called Shanghai Century Longteng, a data center developer, which Hexi held until 2024. That firm owned a controlling 50.1 percent stake in a data center facility called Shenzhen Yifeng Technology Co. Ltd. in mainland China.
The key customer of that data center was Huawei Cloud, the Shenzhen, China-based subsidiary of Huawei Technologies.
In addition, Alice Huang's firm Hexi guaranteed the loans required to finance the Shenzhen data center, which did business with Huawei.
Hexi did not immediately respond to a message via its LinkedIn page sent outside of normal business hours.
CNBC translated corporate records and Chinese news articles in Mandarin that Tesari provided.
It's not clear if the Shenzhen data center was able to acquire Nvidia GPUs, but its majority owner began purchasing the chips in 2023. That company is known as Zhejiang Century Huatong Group and is a business partner of Alice Huang's Hexi through their joint ownership of Century Longteng.
That made Alice Huang a part owner of a data center providing computing power to Huawei. And that was happening at around the same time the first known sightings of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang in public together.
And that raises the question of why Huawei, which has access to Chinese-made chips, would need to rent computing power from an outside entity.
Hexi exited its stake in the data center development company in 2024, but individuals within Alice Huang's network are still connected to the Shenzhen data center. Her husband Kang Wei is a longtime business associate who founded Hexi, where Alice Huang previously held an executive role. In 2022, Kang became an executive of Century Longteng, which owns the controlling stake in the Shenzhen data center, and he also attended the company's signing of the Huawei agreement.

title: Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook and other 365 services
titleJa: Widespread Microsoft outage takes down Outlook and other 365 services
summaryJa: A Microsoft outage on Thursday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365.
bodyOriginal:
Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday that impacted thousands of users across regions, according to outage-tracking website Downdetector.com.
The outage began shortly before 1 p.m. and impacted Microsoft 365 services, Outlook and Teams. At the time, about 130,000 users reported issues with Outlook.
Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site.
"We are aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online," a Microsoft spokesperson wrote in a statement to CNBC. "We appreciate our customers' patience while we work to restore services as soon as possible."
Microsoft shared updates on the outage from its Microsoft 365 Status account on social media platform X.
Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."
At 4 p.m., Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.
"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."
Microsoft initially said infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions" was responsible for the connectivity problems.
The company later determined that the elevated load was caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure" and that some servers were failing automated health checks.
"We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service," Microsoft wrote.

title: Cisco beats on earnings, says AI infrastructure revenue will double this fiscal year
titleJa: Cisco beats on earnings, says AI infrastructure revenue will double this fiscal year
summaryJa: Cisco is trying to become a bigger player in AI after missing out on the early years of the boom.
bodyOriginal:
Cisco shares rose in extended trading on Thursday after the maker of networking gear reported better-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results.
Here's how the company did compared to LSEG consensus estimates:
- EPS: $1.40 adjusted vs. $1.33 expected
- Revenue: $18.5 billion vs. $18.1 billion expected.
Revenue increased 24% from $14.88 billion a year earlier, Cisco said in a statement. Net income rose to $4.6 billion, or $1.14 per share, from $2.9 billion, or 72 center per share, a year ago.
Cisco is trying to gain a foothold in the artificial intelligence buildout after missing out on the early years of the generative AI boom. The company's stock price is up about 35% this year as of Thursday's close, trouncing the Nasdaq, which has gained 9% over that stretch.

title: IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap: What it means for your money
titleJa: IRS announces 2027 401(k) contribution limits, raises savings cap: What it means for your money
summaryJa: The IRS has announced higher 401(k) contribution limits for 2027. Here’s what retirement savers need to know.
bodyOriginal:
The IRS has announced new retirement account contribution limits for 2027.
In its release on Thursday, the agency increased the 401(k) employee deferral limit to $25,500 next year, up from $24,500 in 2026. The change applies to 401(k)s, 403(b)s and most 457 plans, along with the federal Thrift Savings Plan.
The IRS also unveiled 2027 catch-up contribution limits for savers age 50 and older, new individual retirement account savings limits and higher income thresholds for Roth IRA contributions.
Starting in 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution limit will rise to $8,500 for savers 50 and older, up from $8,000 in 2026. But investors aged 60 to 63 can instead save an extra $11,750, based on changes enacted via Secure 2.0. That figure is up $500 from 2026.
Both amounts are in addition to the $25,500 deferral limit for 2027.
The 2027 IRA contribution limit is $7,500, unchanged from 2026, the IRS announced. IRA catch-up contributions for investors age 50 and older will be $1,100, the same as 2026.
The announcement comes one week after the agency released dozens of other inflation adjustments for 2027, including federal income tax brackets, higher capital gains brackets, estate and gift tax exemptions and provisions impacting families, among others.
Get your 401(k) employer match first
In 2025, only 14% of participants maxed out their 401(k)s, according to Vanguard's 2026 How America Saves report, which was based on data from more than 1,300 qualified plans and nearly 5 million participants. The average combined savings rate, including employer deposits, was an estimated 12.1%, according to the same report.
"Before worrying about contribution limits, make sure you're capturing your full employer match," said Sean Michael Pearson, a certified financial planner with Ameriprise Financial Services in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania.
During the second quarter of 2026, about 19% of employees weren't deferring enough to 401(k)s to receive their company's full matching contribution, according to a Fidelity analysis of 27,300 corporate plans and nearly 26 million participants.
Vanguard suggests saving 12% to 15% of your pay per year, including employer contributions, depending on your income. But only one-quarter of 401(k) participants deferred more than 10% of earnings in 2025, according to Vanguard's report.
If you plan to max out your 401(k) for 2027, you should change your savings rate in December so it's active by your first January paycheck, experts say. The update could take one or two pay periods to go into effect.
Boost your 401(k) savings rate every year
The "most important habit" is consistently increasing your 401(k) savings rate over time, according to Pearson.
For example, if you bump 401(k) contributions by 1% every year, "you may barely notice the difference in your paycheck, but the long-term impact can be substantial," he said.
In 2025, about 27% of 401(k) plans automatically increased employee deferrals over time, known as "auto-escalation," according to the Plan Sponsor Council of America's yearly survey of 401(k)s. The nonprofit trade organization's survey included 753 plans.
The vast majority of plans with auto-escalation, 69%, boosted deferrals by 1% per year, the Plan Sponsor Council of America found.

title: Analysis: Jensen Huang’s exit tests Nvidia’s role as the ‘central bank of AI’
titleJa: Analysis: Jensen Huang’s exit tests Nvidia’s role as the ‘central bank of AI’
summaryJa: The tech giant's web of ties to other companies is raising the possibility that it could do far-reaching economic and financial damage.
bodyOriginal:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's shock resignation is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom?
Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system.
Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector.
A rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis isn't likely, according to analysts and current and former financial officials. Nvidia isn't "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," said Sheila Bair, a former government regulator who ran the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Unlike a troubled bank, Nvidia isn't vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and would still produce a product customers want to buy even if something went wrong. And its massive equity gives it a cushion.
But regulators need to watch carefully for exposure by the banks and the wider financial system to Nvidia and other firms like it, Bair said.
"Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event," she said.
Investors still have high hopes for Nvidia, which reports earnings on Tuesday. Analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year, and then to roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data. But Huang's exit from the company Thursday following a pair of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman The New York Times reported was suspected of spying for China, makes the company's fate extraordinarily hard to predict. Huang had led the company since co-founding it in 1993.
Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment. The company named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
Nvidia's stock fell 33% from its Oct. 6 peak through Thursday morning. Still, people who closely track the financial flows underlying AI say that even sharper losses by Nvidia likely wouldn't trigger the kind of systemic problems that regulators guard against.
And yet the risks flowing from AI are keeping some finance officials up at night. They are watching for the possibility that many of the factors that have helped the AI boom could reverse simultaneously. If the value of Nvidia's GPU chips fell, for instance, it could prompt investors to ask whether companies that borrowed money to buy them would be able to pay off their debts.
In that case, the financial assistance big tech firms have extended to others in the industry could suddenly become drags on their growth. Tech companies would have credit problems at the same time that their equity is falling. Problems among giant tech firms wouldn't stay contained to tech investors' portfolios, but could cause problems across the economy.
"I think that's a real concern because both the economy and financial markets are standing on the same leg, which means a drawdown could have reinforcing effects between the two," said Jason Wu, an assistant director at the International Monetary Fund who oversees the Global Markets Analysis unit.
Wu was the lead author of a chapter of the IMF's Global Financial Stability report published in October that warned about the potential for growing leverage among AI firms and investors to trigger broader problems. The so-called hyperscalers — the biggest tech firms — have grown from just 1% of bond issuance in the $15 trillion investment-grade debt market to 10% in just two years. Hedge funds and retail investors are making risky bets even riskier by taking on debt to buy stocks or investing in funds that have embedded leverage.
Nvidia is at the center of all of that. The company has repeatedly stepped in to help backstop smaller AI companies known as neoclouds, which build data centers using Nvidia chips and lease capacity to other firms. Among other obligations, Nvidia disclosed in July that it has committed to buy up to $36 billion in cloud services from those companies. That helps Nvidia ensure that there will be more customers for its AI chips, and it helps those companies find easier financing.
Wu and others refer to these kinds of arrangements as circular financing. When business is growing, it can be productive for bigger firms to help their customers buy their products. But if Nvidia couldn't honor its obligations, it would ripple through the firms that borrowed the money and the banks that lent to it. Relatively opaque private credit funds have also lent heavily into the AI boom, and how they would fare is a subject of debate among regulators.
Nvidia didn't reveal its specific partners, but some neoclouds such as CoreWeave and IREN have separately disclosed their relationships with the bigger firm.
Many neoclouds have been under stress in recent weeks. The cost of insuring CoreWeave debt, as measured by credit-default spreads, rose by 94% — nearly doubling — from Oct. 1 to Nov. 5, before settling, according to LSEG data. The price of an IREN convertible bond maturing in 2029 fell 23% from Nov. 3 to Nov. 5, amid a 26% decline in the company's share price.
Nvidia's other obligations include a $105 billion phased guarantee to a major data center project in Ohio planned by OpenAI and SB Energy, subject to certain conditions. Nvidia promised to backstop up to $125 billion of a $500 billion credit program by Wall Street financial firms.
These obligations come in different forms and are unlikely to come due all at once, if ever. Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a Columbia Business School finance professor, estimates them at $400 billion overall.
That is a huge sum, but still a small fraction of the roughly $3.9 trillion market capitalization Nvidia has even after its stock decline. "The company would have to get to the brink of extinction before all these guarantees come into jeopardy."
"I don't want to say it's a safe system, but I do want to say there's a lot of equity in the system right now," Van Nieuwerburgh said.
But in the past few days, Nvidia's troubles have separated it from the pack. Most neoclouds' equity prices have recovered this week as Nvidia's share price has fallen. That suggests investors see Nvidia's problems as specific to the company, for now.
Meanwhile the basic laws of economics are driving other firms to try to move into Nvidia's lucrative chips business. AMD, Broadcom, Intel, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI all have efforts underway to build their own AI chips, Van Nieuwerburgh said.
Over time, they could replace Nvidia's products. That could cap the economic fallout of any potential troubles at the company.
And yet it's impossible to entirely write off the financial risks of the AI trade suddenly hitting a wall, added Van Nieuwerburgh, who spoke to me over Zoom from the sidelines of a bimonthly meeting of finance officials in Basel, Switzerland.
Central bankers "are clearly very, very, very anxious about this and thinking hard about these questions," he said.

title: Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's permanent chief executive?
titleJa: Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's permanent chief executive?
summaryJa: Chief financial officer Colette Kress will replace him temporarily, but several others are in the frame as potential successors.
bodyOriginal:
Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's permanent chief executive?
- Published
Nvidia is now facing a scenario few would have considered until very recently - a future without Jensen Huang.
The chief executive and co-founder of the AI chip-making giant is at the centre of a major scandal over reports of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
On Thursday, Nvidia's board announced he had resigned effective immediately.
He will be replaced, for now, by Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress.
The tech giant is facing one of its biggest challenges, finding the right person to permanently lead the business that Huang helped create more than three decades ago and turned into one of the world's most valuable companies.
We take a look at which candidates have emerged as potential successors.
The finance chief
Nvidia's finance chief, Colette Kress, is taking on the chief executive role for an interim period while the company searches for a permanent replacement.
An industry veteran for more than 30 years, Kress previously held high positions at tech firms like Cisco and Microsoft.
Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's executive vice president, has seen the firm's transformation from making chips for video games in the early 1990s to becoming an AI semiconductor powerhouse.
She "fronts every earnings call" alongside Huang and is a "familiar and trusted voice for the market at a time when it badly needs one," said Josh Gilbert, an analyst at investment firm eToro.
But doing the job permanently could be a different story, said Gilbert, as the firm, known for its edge in technology, could want an engineer in the chair.
The co-founder and the engineer
Another option is Chris Malachowsky, who founded Nvidia alongside Huang and Curtis Priem, and is the only executive that shares the same level of seniority.
Malachowsky has played a key part in developing the company's computing technology.
Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's high-performance computing business, has also emerged as a potential candidate if the company is keen to put an engineer in the top job.
Buck was among the early pioneers who helped popularise the use of graphic processors beyond gaming applications.
"He could protect Nvidia's technological edge, but his ability to manage the wider commercial relationships and geopolitical challenges would face scrutiny," said Charu Chanana, investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.
Today, Nvidia's leading processors are widely regarded as the gold standard for AI development.
Huang's children also work at Nvidia in executive positions but are relatively young and inexperienced.
Apple and Arm's top brass
Nvidia is likely to favour an internal appointment initially but could look externally for a more permanent replacement, said Jun Bei Liu, founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap.
Several names of tech entrepreneurs outside of Nvidia have been floated by experts.
Liu said Apple's former chief executive, Tim Cook, could be a possible choice as someone familiar with managing global supply chains, though she questioned whether he would be willing to leave the iPhone maker, where he is the chair.
Liu and Chanana also suggested Rene Haas, chief executive of Arm Holdings, the UK chipmaking giant.
Nvidia's processors are made with the help of chipmakers around the world, including Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung.
Haas is familiar with leading a publicly-listed company and would bring semiconductor experience, though Nvidia's business model is considerably different from Arm's, said Chanana.
"The challenge is finding someone who can combine Jensen's technical understanding, strategic vision and relationships across the global technology industry," Liu said.
Where now for Huang?
Ten Cap's Liu had believed it was just a matter of time before Huang would step down as Nvidia's chief executive.
"The issue is no longer simply about personal conduct," she said. "It is about corporate governance, national security concerns and maintaining confidence in the leadership of one of the world's most strategically important companies."
Several major investment firms have downgraded their forecasts for the chip giant - a rare shift given investors' longstanding optimism about the company.
Stacy Rasgon, senior analyst in US semiconductors at Bernstein Research, wrote in a note to investors that "our gut tells us we probably haven't fully probed the depths of what might be found here".
Rasgon halved Bernstein's share price target for Nvidia and said: "We've had enough and prefer to watch from the sidelines."
Ray Wang, chief executive of Constellation Research, said the crisis isn't so much an issue for the wider AI industry but rather one for Nvidia itself which has to consider if the person it appoints as its chief executive has the same appeal as Huang.
"That's really what the issue is, because a lot of these partnerships and investments have been made because of the trust with with Jensen," he said.
Additional reporting by Kali Hays

title: Nvidia stock falls nearly 10% as CEO Jensen Huang announces resignation
titleJa: Nvidia stock falls nearly 10% as CEO Jensen Huang announces resignation
summaryJa: Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed.
bodyOriginal:
Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% on Thursday, sending the company's value below $4 trillion in market cap after Jensen Huang announced he would immediately step down as CEO and a member of the board at the chipmaker.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO until a new leader is appointed, Nvidia said in a Thursday statement. Harvey C. Jones, former CEO of Synopsys, will become the first-ever chair of the board.
On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an affair. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed, according to The Financial Times, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China.
The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Huang had another extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Powell reports to Huang, according to the Times.
Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that this departure could lead the stock to fall 20%, given how critical he has been to Nvidia's success. Nvidia's stock is already down more than 20% over the last month.
Bernstein on Thursday slashed its price target on Nvidia's stock by half from $400 to $200.

Robert Greifeld, former Nasdaq chairman and CEO

"If there's a new CEO in, they don't have to make any decisions day one, day 30, day 60. They have time to really get their footing and come up with their own strategic vision," he told CNBC. "You're not going to change what is in the development plan for chips that exists today. So I think certainly it would be a loss, but given the nature of the business and the long lead time for these chip developments and the long contractual relationships they have with customers, it would give them certainly room to maneuver."
Questar Capital Partners
CIO Richard Reyle told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" that Nvidia's board had painted themselves into a corner by not having any kind of succession plan in place.
"I've heard him compared to Steve Jobs being removed from Apple, but [Jobs] put in place a succession plan and cultivated and groomed Tim Cook for years, so that when he passed away and [Cook] took over, there was a real leader there," he said. "Right now, Nvidia doesn't have that person in place, so it's going to be a choice of keeping Jensen and being faced with … all kinds of interrogations, or they're going to have to move on from him, and that's just going to make the stock uninvestable. UBS
"NVIDIA upheaval puts tech concentration risks in focus," Mark Haefele, global wealth management chief investment officer at UBS, and his team said on Thursday morning.
"Without taking any views on individual companies, the episode reinforces the importance of investment diversification and selectivity as the AI trade matures. We retain our conviction in AI's long-term potential, with compute demand remaining robust and earnings resilient. But elevated expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes can leave concentrated portfolios exposed to company-specific setbacks."
Wind Shift Capital
"Jensen Huang is toast," Bill Blain, founder and principal, said in his morning newsletter. "Nvidia's dependence on Jensen Huang is now exposed as a major market risk. The dominant firm within the AI industry lacks clear succession planning and Huang was seen as the acceptable face of AI by the public."
"Confidence in the AI sector has been wobbling for months," he added. "Huang's departure could lead to instability and trigger another collapse."

titleJa: Nvidia's CEO was the rock star of AI before his dramatic unravelling
summaryJa: Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global AI race has crumbled.
bodyOriginal:
Nvidia's CEO was the rock star of AI before his dramatic unravelling
- Published
In recent years, Jensen Huang has been riding high on the crest of the AI wave as his company Nvidia became one of the most valuable in the world.
It only took a few days for it to all come crashing down.
Back-to-back revelations of two affairs involving the CEO, including a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, upended his seemingly untouchable status as a leading tech figure and led to his resignation from the company he helped form.
His departure leaves uncertainty in the global stock market, which leans on his microchip company, and over the future of a US company seen as a linchpin in the country's race for AI dominance over China.
On Wednesday, reports emerged that the 63-year-old married man was said to have had an affair with a Nvidia colleague, coming just days after revelations surfaced of a romantic relationship with a woman alleged to be a spy for China.
This hit the company's shares, and they sank again after the New York Times reported that Huang had had a second affair with an executive at his own company.
Huang is well known in the technology, business and political world, but despite his company's rocketing rise over the past four years, he perhaps isn't as big a household name as fellow tech bros Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerburg.
However, Huang is probably more consequential to the development of AI across the world due to Nvidia making the best microchips in the business, which are used to power the technology.
The company, which is still valued at more than $4 trillion despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
This has led to Huang holding court with both US President Donald Trump and China's President XI Jinping. The leather-jacket wearing CEO has access to the world's powerful like few others.
His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn (£109bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
Despite always donning his trademark black leather jacket look, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his current wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work at their father's firm.
He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan, he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff.
The company became a key provider of computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in direction and entered the world of AI. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing technology.
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity.
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with Trump. At a recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Huang and Musk.
It was no surprise that Huang was at the top table. Companies using Nvidia's chips include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic.
In essence, Huang's customer base includes the biggest firms on the planet and they are spending plenty on Nvidia's products.
This intertwining of companies means that the negative impact being felt by Nvidia, on the stock market for example, could perhaps have wider implications on other companies and the wider economy.
Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, and that it was "very important to him".
"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
After the revelations of the first affair, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.
Trump, as well as other leaders in the AI tech industry, had backed Huang to continue in his role at Nvidia. The president described him as "honourable".

The company, which is still valued at more than $4 trillion despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
This has led to Huang holding court with both US President Donald Trump and China's President XI Jinping. The leather-jacket wearing CEO has access to the world's powerful like few others.
His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn (£109bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
Despite always donning his trademark black leather jacket look, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his current wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work at their father's firm.
He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan, he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff.
The company became a key provider of computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in direction and entered the world of AI. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing technology.
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity.
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with Trump. At a recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Huang and Musk.
It was no surprise that Huang was at the top table. Companies using Nvidia's chips include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic.
In essence, Huang's customer base includes the biggest firms on the planet and they are spending plenty on Nvidia's products.
This intertwining of companies means that the negative impact being felt by Nvidia, on the stock market for example, could perhaps have wider implications on other companies and the wider economy.
Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, and that it was "very important to him".
"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
After the revelations of the first affair, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.
Trump, as well as other leaders in the AI tech industry, had backed Huang to continue in his role at Nvidia. The president described him as "honourable".

title: Trump says ‘we don’t need a deal with Iran’

title: Faisal Islam: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
titleJa: Faisal Islam: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient

bodyOriginal:
Faisal Islam: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
- Published
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.
"Top gear" and "strikingly strong" were among the descriptions of the 0.7% growth offered by the economists who track every minor murmur of Britain's economy.
It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient", and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War".
Against the backdrop of the world's biggest disruption to energy flows, rising market borrowing costs - and the cruel summers since the pandemic - it is impressive growth.
It should reset some of the swirl of self-reinforcing negativity.
The UK's economic growth has averaged less than 0.1% in the four Q3s [ie July to September] since the pandemic.
The average prediction just months ago for this July to September was just 0.1%.
Even the UK's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) effectively pencilled in 0.3% at the Budget just 3 weeks ago.
This figure has not been exceeded outside the pandemic since 2017. It puts the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy after the US across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.
It is tempting to think about what the economy would have done if the Iran War hadn't happened. If interest rates had been cut instead of their recent rise.
Not a boom
While the latest figure kills the doom, it is clearly not a boom either.
Spending on AI and tech have driven the surprise upside over the year. While the AI data centre boom may at any point turn to bust, these figures suggest that spending across the economy on investing in these technologies is helping to boost growth. Consumers have been resilient, at least till the autumn, perhaps helped by better economic vibes.
While there has been an understandable focus on high UK borrowing costs, another measure of the international standing of the UK economy, sterling's value, reached post Brexit referendum highs last week.
Productivity and investment is also looking stronger, especially after recent revisions. Some of the most encouraging figures are in private sector business investment.
I spoke to the chancellor at Nexeon in Oxfordshire, which is searching for a UK factory to manufacture its cutting edge electric vehicle battery - and British - technology. My colleagues visited British watchmakers in Maidenhead carving out a niche to take on the Swiss.
However, this may well not last for the final three months of the year.
Consumer confidence has already fallen as petrol and domestic energy prices start to rise again.
There is a significant challenge with everyday cost-of-living pressures in the coming months. Construction and private house building remain depressed.
The Iran conflict remains the big unknown and whether post the US midterm elections there could be a durable end to the conflict in the Gulf.
Some oil and gas production there is starting to normalise. It could bring down petrol prices, energy bills, government borrowing costs, and mortgage costs too.
Expect to see Downing Street investing heavily in "settlement of the conflict", which the chancellor told me is the "best economic policy".

title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
titleJa: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
summaryJa: ﻿The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to September, according to official figures.
bodyOriginal:
UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
- Published
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.
Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures, external show.
The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.
Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.
Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.
The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.
Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.
But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.
However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".
"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.
Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".
Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.
Although investors have recently been concerned about slower artificial intelligence development in the US and the long term viability of AI firms' business models, businesses have continued to invest in the technologies.
Sarah Coles, from investment platform AJ Bell, said that since the start of the year, "it's the less visible back-office work that has delivered, with administrative and supportive services seeing strong growth" noting that these are the areas benefitting from the increasing use of AI.
The latest figures put the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.
However, Jake Finney, senior economist at consultancy PwC, cautioned that growth was likely to slow over the coming months "unless energy markets stabilise".
A sharp rise in energy bills is forecast for January, which is likely to hit consumer spending and confidence, he said.
High energy costs have been stoked by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
US and Israeli attacks led to Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz - a vital shipping route for the world's oil and gas.
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine have been attacking each other's oil refineries, leading to a squeeze on global refining capacity, hitting diesel and petrol prices.
What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you?
- Published5 hours ago
'Surprising resilience'
Richard Benc, founder of mechanical watch company Studio Underdog, says sales are better than he expected.
"We've seen more resilience than we had forecast for and expected. We are still projecting growth this year," he says.
The business exports about 80% of its watches. "We've seen a surprising amount of resilience, particularly from our US customers," he adds, although some UK customers are now taking longer to buy watches.

title: Nvidia prepares to oust Jensen Huang, WSJ reports — stock sinks
titleJa: Nvidia prepares to oust Jensen Huang, WSJ reports — stock sinks
summaryJa: The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy.
bodyOriginal:
Shares of Nvidia fell more than 9% in after-hours trading on Wednesday after The Wall Street Journal reported that the company's board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang.
The news landed minutes after The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with another executive at the company. Nvidia's board is preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang's future at the company, according to the Journal.
The alleged relationship was with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia, according to the Times' report. Powell's bio on the Nvidia website says she's "responsible for the company's worldwide healthcare business, including hardware and software platforms for accelerated computing, AI, and visualization that power the ecosystem of medical imaging, life sciences, drug discovery, and healthcare analytics."
Huang and Powell were reportedly captured on camera being affectionate with one another at a hotel in San Jose, California in March, according to the Times.
Nvidia and Powell did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Heller, the crisis PR firm Huang reportedly hired as early as last year, did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
The report comes days after Huang admitted to an affair with a woman who is believed by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The CEO was romantically involved with Alice Huang, according to The Financial Times, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, The New York Times reported.
Nvidia's board of directors has opened an independent investigation and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to look into the spying allegations.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," Huang wrote in the message to Nvidia staff on Sunday. "I am deeply sorry."
Most of Huang's Nvidia shares are co-owned with his wife, Lori Huang, and are held in trusts. About 800 million shares are held by those trusts. Huang holds about 70 million shares on his own and has limited economic control over the company.
Rumors of an affair between Huang and Powell have circulated for years, in part because Powell lacks a background in health or science, according to a former employee who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter.
Healthcare is a smaller business at Nvidia. The company makes chips for medical devices and MRI machines, but they are a minor in comparison to the revenue generated from its advanced AI systems and graphics processing units, or GPUs. In recent appearances, including at the company's annual GTC conference, Powell has spoken about how Nvidia's AI technology can help accelerate drug discovery, assist providers and improve clinical efficiency. Powell has been leading the group since 2017.
Nvidia's stock was down 7% this week prior to the after-hours drop on Wednesday and is on pace for its sixth straight weekly slide, reflecting broad concern on the sustainability of the artificial intelligence buildout. The AI infrastructure trade was hit particularly hard last week after the midterm elections, as Democrats won sweeping majorities in both houses of Congress, and dozens of ballot measures past that could make building data centers more difficult.
Huang has become synonymous with the AI industry, and he is often referred to by his first name ,"Jensen," by customers and rivals. Nvidia has been one of the primary beneficiaries of the AI boom since its chips are used to train models and run large AI workloads.
—CNBC's Lora Kolodny and Kif Leswing contributed to this report
